To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Unruh–De Witt detector model, which has been used in a large number of studies, is not suitable for the study of detector–field correlations, but the model can be fixed by adding a counterterm that accounts for the backreaction of the field on the detector.

(1) linear perturbation theory, when properly applied to detector-field interactions, is a very useful tool in extracting detector-detector, field-field and detector-field correlations from a quantum field theory; and (2) backreaction effects from the quantum field on detector behavior are important in determining detector-detector and detector-field correlations, and are not always negligible, even in the limit of weak coupling between the detector and the quantum field.

(i) the detector–field correlation function is not the same as the detector–field commutator; (ii) detector–detector correlations are not the same as field–field correlations; (iii) the backreaction effects on detector–detector correlations can be large, but not as large as the backreaction effects for detector–field correlations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantum information aspects of the relativistic dynamics of quantum systems, with particular emphasis on the quantum entanglement of the systems.
the study of the interaction of relativistic quantum systems with their environment.
the development of a quantum information theory of relativistic detectors in a quantum field theory context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, while linear perturbation theory is useful for obtaining the first approximation of detector–detector, detector–field and field–field correlation functions, the backreaction effects from the quantum field on a detector’s behavior must be accounted for to obtain accurate results.
the Unruh–De-Witt detector model, in spite of its simplicity and limitations, is a very useful tool for the analysis of relativistic quantum information in detectors–field interactions.
the backreaction is a crucial element for understanding the physics of the detector–field interactions in relativistic quantum field theories.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the linear perturbation theory is not always a valid approximation in the relativistic quantum field setting, and the backreaction effects should be considered in the analysis of detector–field interactions.

, while perturbative results are valid and reliable for a wide range of situations, they do not provide the full story, and nonperturbative results can give us additional insights into detector–field interaction physics.

the quantum information dynamics of the detector–field system can be fully captured by a non-Markovian master equation, which can be derived from a nonperturbative analysis of the detector–quantum field interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the backreaction effects are important for a complete characterization of the detector dynamics.

, in the relativistic context, the backreaction is a crucial effect which cannot be neglected, even in the case of very weak couplings, and it can lead to very interesting effects, such as the appearance of nonlocality in the detector–detector and detector–field entanglement dynamics.
backreaction effects are not negligible, and can be important even at low temperatures.
